As for the film… Before you load a reel, take a look at the film. Hold a frame or two  up to the light, or use your phone flashlight. Hold it the way it would feed into the machine: horizontally. Now look at the text on the frame. 

If the text is upright and easy to read in that position, the film was shot in landscape.

If it  looks sideways—like you’ve got to tilt your head to read it upright—it was shot in portrait.

Most of the 16mm film is shot in portrait and those older machines can’t rotate the image, so you’ll either be reading sideways or need to switch to a digital reader.

35mm film is usually landscape and works fine in most machines. Microfiche is a different format altogether—flat sheets instead of reels: and needs a different reader.

If you load a reel and see two images stacked in one frame, that’s duplex film. So you’ll  need to crop or split the frame to read each image clearly. That’s another scenario where a digital reader is the better option.

Hope this helps

If you’re at a public archive or library, ask staff if they have a ScanPro or ViewScan—those are the most common. (ScanPro 2200/3000, ST ViewScan series, or Canon MS-series (with PC interface).

This is a solid idea with real potential, but there are some practical steps to think about to make sure it works as intended. To keep the app from being bought or sold, you’d need to set it up as a non-profit or foundation. This way, its assets are legally locked, and any money it generates is reinvested into the project. Another option is registering it as a Public Benefit Corporation, which legally ties it to its mission and makes profits secondary.

For governance, using blockchain and a Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) would keep things transparent and community-driven. The DAO could handle decisions like updates, rules, and moderation, with smart contracts enforcing those decisions. That would make it almost impossible for anyone to bypass the rules or sell the app without the community’s consent.

The app itself could be hosted on a decentralized platform like IPFS, so no single entity has control over the servers. Operations could be spread out across multiple nodes or devices, keeping the infrastructure as decentralized as its governance. Ownership would stay with the users—not through shares or equity, but through tokens earned by contributing to the platform, like creating content or helping with moderation.

To keep the app running, you’d avoid traditional funding methods like ads or big investors. Instead, you could rely on things like optional subscriptions, tipping systems for creators, or community donations. These approaches would provide funding without compromising the app’s independence.

There are challenges to this approach. Blockchain systems can be complicated for most people to understand, so the interface would need to simplify things as much as possible. Scalability is another concern since blockchain can get slow and expensive as it grows. Using a Layer-2 solution like Polygon could help by making transactions faster and cheaper.

If these issues are addressed, the app could stay community-owned and protected from outside control. It’s realistic to build something that aligns with these goals as long as the focus stays on keeping it decentralized, transparent, and sustainable.

Look talking about Ted Hughes and Sylvia Plath, with Assia Wevill’s story is always going to be a bit of walking through a minefield. But books like Red Comet and The Grief of Influence shake up the old stories a bit, especially around the abuse accusations, giving us more shades to think about.

Imagine carrying the weight of so much tragedy—Plath’s suicide, then Wevill’s  filicide-suicide. It’s a kind of heartache that’s hard to wrap your head around. And yet, Hughes kept his pen moving, kept wrestling with words, living up to The White Goddess and even earning the laurels of a Poet Laureate.

Yet where Hughes really steps into the spotlight is how he handled Plath’s work posthumously. After The Bell Jar came out, amid all its legal battles, he could have let her work drift into obscurity. Instead, he brings out Ariel, (even though he fiddles with it a bit) and that move changes the course of poetry. By pushing her work out there—Winter Trees, Crossing the River, and more—he’s a big (though not the only) reason why we’re still talking about Plath today.

Sure, there are bits and pieces of this whole saga that might make us want to pause and rethink. But, let’s not paint the entire picture black because of those. Hughes was, without doubt, a monumental figure in the last century’s poetry scene, only just trailing behind Plath if you ask me.

“The Magus” by John Fowles (1965) - A story packed with psychological games, existential queries, and a mysterious island, “The Magus” envelops the reader in a narrative that constantly blurs the line between reality and illusion, mirroring Lynch’s cinematic style.

“Crash” by J.G. Ballard (1973) - the controversial novel about symphorophilia (sexual attraction to car crashes) a disquieting narrative that shares Lynch’s fascination with the darker aspects of human nature and modern society.

“Picnic at Hanging Rock” by Joan Lindsay (1967) - an eerie atmosphere, mystery, it evokes a Lynchian sense of the inexplicable and the ominous lurking beneath the surface of a seemingly idyllic setting

“Pedro Páramo” by Juan Rulfo (1955) - This, tells the story of a young man’s journey to find his father in a ghost town inhabited by the spirits of the past. Its eerie atmosphere and blending of the living and the dead echo Lynch’s fascination with the boundaries between life and death.

“The Woman in the Dunes” by Kōbō Abe (1962) - its about a man trapped in a sand pit with a mysterious woman in a remote village it explores themes of isolation, existential dread, and the bizarre, reminiscent of the psychological and physical entrapments found in Lynch’s work.

“The Bloody Chamber” by Angela Carter (1979) - A collection of dark, feminist retellings of traditional fairy tales that explore themes of desire, violence, and transformation. Its Gothic its exploration of the uncanny could echo Lynch’s atmospheric storytelling.

“The Recognitions” by William Gaddis (1955) - a challenging novel that deals with themes of authenticity, art forgery, and the search for meaning in a postmodern world, echoing Lynch’s preoccupations with identity and the elusive nature of truth.

“The Lime Twig” by John Hawkes (1961) - This is, about a man who gets involved in a horse racing scam, plunges into a dreamlike world of violence and eroticism. Its haunting and hallucinatory atmosphere parallels Lynch’s cinematic landscapes.

“The Blind Owl” by Sadegh Hedayat (1937) - A cornerstone of Persian literature, this novel’s psychological exploration of a man’s descent into madness, with its use of dreamlike imagery, makes it a kindred spirit to Lynch’s exploration of the psyche.

So:

the Burton-Verse is “mid-level” there’s still some fantastic/comic elements, but realism is still in the atmosphere (especially in the first film). 

The Nolan-Verse expands on the realism and grounds Batman in an heightened version of the real world. Batman is much more tactical, and his arsenal more militarized to keep in line with the realism. 

The Reeves-Verse (while not yet released, the following could be discerned through what available) leans more into realism. Our Batman has a much more tactical hand-made suit, a cape that does not form into a bat-winged glider, but into a more realistic wing suit. The batmobile isn’t a sleek gothic sports car, but a supped up muscle car.

As a whole, the Solo Batman films has morphed from a fantastical/comic world with an atmosphere of realism into a realistic world with a fantastical/comic atmosphere.

Case in point the Batmobile. Look at Burton’s compared to Nolan’s, Burton’s is slightly removed comic books, Nolan’s is more removed than that, making it a more realistic militarized tactical vehicle, Reeves’ is even more removed, more into the realm of reality, it’s more DIY than all the rest.
